title: Iberieli
headline: One winery, two websites, the same developer
summary: A family winery's site, built by hand in 2024 and rebuilt in 2026 so the family can manage their own wine catalogue and importers abroad can find where to buy.
role: Freelance developer: design, build, and ongoing support

timeline.text: First website: designed in Figma, tested with users, hand-coded in English and Georgian.
Paid revisions: SEO passes and content updates as the wine range grew.
Full rebuild on Next.js with a database and an admin panel the family uses themselves.

tldr: Iberieli is a family-owned Georgian winery making natural wine in qvevri, selling mostly to importers abroad.
I built their first website in 2024 and came back in 2026 to rebuild it as a server-rendered Next.js site with its own wine catalogue admin.
Today the family adds, edits and hides wines without a developer, every wine has its own searchable page, and each visitor sees distributors in their country.

sections.heading: The client
paragraphs: Iberieli is a small family business. They grow grapes, make wine the traditional Georgian way, and sell to importers and distributors in other countries. Their website isn't a shop. It's the thing a buyer in Germany or Japan opens after a wine fair to decide whether this winery is serious.
So it has to look trustworthy, explain each wine properly (grapes, vinification, taste, food pairing), and make it obvious how to buy.

sections.heading: 2024: the first version
paragraphs: I started in February 2024, working directly with the head of the business. We designed in Figma, tested the layout with a few people outside the company, and I hand-coded the site in HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in English and Georgian. It went live in mid-2024 on free hosting, so there was no monthly cost to the winery.
It did its job, but every new wine, new photo or corrected description needed me. As the range grew, that became the bottleneck.

sections.heading: 2026: the rebuild
paragraphs: When the family asked for more changes, I suggested we stop patching and rebuild properly. These are the main decisions:
bullets: A wine catalogue in a database, with a simple admin panel. The family can add a wine, upload photos, edit tasting notes, mark organic farming, and hide a wine that's sold out without deleting it.
Server-rendered pages. Every wine page arrives as complete HTML, which search engines and link previews read correctly.
Each wine has its own page with its own title, description, social preview and product data. A search for one specific wine can lead straight to it.
"Where to buy" adapts to the visitor's country. A visitor from Poland sees the Polish distributor first, without a location pop-up.
Privacy-friendly analytics. Measurement only loads after the visitor accepts cookies, so the family can see which wines get attention.

sections.heading: What changed for the business
paragraphs: The website is no longer something the winery waits on. Updating the catalogue now takes minutes, done by the people who know the wine best. When I'm involved now, it's to add new capabilities, not to fix a typo.

underTheHood.heading: Under the hood
paragraphs: Next.js 16 App Router with server components, Neon serverless Postgres through Drizzle ORM, Cloudinary for images, and a small custom authentication system (JWT sessions with hashed passwords) instead of a third-party auth provider. That keeps the running cost close to zero for a business this size.
bullets: Geo-aware distributors: a tiny API route reads the country header that the hosting platform already attaches to every request. No geolocation permission and no third-party IP lookup.
Structured data: Organization, WebSite and a Product schema per wine, plus a generated sitemap and a robots file that keeps the admin out of search.
Hide, don't delete: a visibility flag lets the family pause a wine and bring it back next vintage without losing its page.

cta: Have a business that needs a website you can run yourself?
